title: Displaced persons
hookLine: survivors wait in camps for somewhere to go

cards: A camp in Germany, after the war. Wooden barracks, sometimes old army buildings, sometimes the same kind of fences. But today there's a wedding in one of the halls.
The bride's dress, the story goes, was sewn from parachute silk. Someone has found a fiddle. Someone has baked something that is almost a cake.
Outside, the same barracks, the same fence, the same waiting. Inside, people dance. Today's word is the plain official name for the people in that hall.

teach.b: The Allies had a bureaucratic term for people the war had torn from home: displaced persons, DPs for short. Jewish survivors who could not or would not go back ended up in DP camps in Germany, Austria and Italy.

teach.h: HOME WAS GONE; SHIPS STOPPED AT SEA.
teach.b: Because home was gone. Families had been murdered. Houses and shops had been taken by others.
And in some towns, survivors who returned were met with hostility, even violence. So people came back to the camps, or never left them. Other doors opened slowly, when they opened at all.
The British, who then ruled Palestine, held Jewish immigration under tight limits, and ships carrying survivors there were stopped at sea. So the survivors waited, and waiting, they lived.
They called themselves by a Hebrew name, She'erit Hapletah: the surviving remnant. They opened schools and printed newspapers, staged plays, held elections, trained to farm.
They married, and babies were born in the barracks.

teach.h: BUILD YE HOUSES, AND DWELL IN THEM.
teach.b: The prophet Jeremiah once wrote a letter to exiles in Babylon, people waiting far from home, and told them not to put their lives on hold: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them." Plant gardens, he wrote. Marry.
Raise children where you are. The survivors in the camps did something like that. They had a roof, and food, and each other.
What they didn't have was a place that was theirs. Nowhere to go is not the same as nothing to do.

how: Some Jewish families keep photographs and documents from the DP camps where their parents or grandparents waited, and Jewish organizations that once aided DPs still work with refugees today.

games.q: you're a survivor in a DP camp. your town is no longer home, and no country has opened its doors yet. what do you do?
o: go back to your old town anyway.
build a life in the camp while you wait.
games.why: survivors opened schools, printed newspapers, married and raised babies in the barracks while they waited for a place.

practice: Bring to mind people waiting right now for somewhere to go, in camps, at borders, in shelters, sleeping in cars, and picture one ordinary detail: a bag packed and repacked, a child doing homework on a cot, a phone charging in a hallway.
Stay with that one detail. If you pray, pray for people waiting for a place; if not, hold them in mind with care.

wordCard.voice: Displaced persons. The official name for people the war tore from home. For Jewish survivors, it meant long waits in camps for somewhere to go.

orig.note: Hebrew: the surviving remnant, the name the survivors gave themselves.

carryVoice: Your line: nowhere to go. They built a life in the waiting room anyway. Go gently.
